name: Jamal Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel; we have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. Your answers are confidential, so what is your work like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a small carpentry crew restoring old roofs, and today we are replacing a rotten oak beam in a church. My vocational trade certificate started me on site, and years of repairs taught me to read damp timber. I scan the roof and use AI modelling daily, then check the cut list by hand.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Lucia works at a dental clinic, our children are grown, and we own our house with more than six months saved. This trade pays me well, and there are plenty of building jobs nearby, though the exact wages differ. I sell a few handmade tables from my garage workshop, and I enjoy trying a new tool when I can test it safely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the restoration crew our roof scanner still saves me paperwork, and the old beams still need hands. I would post a photograph of the scarf joint we finished at the mill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our timber repair contracts look healthy and my partner Lucia has steady dental clinic work. We have the house and more than six months saved, and there are other building firms nearby if this one slows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading the church roof repair and checking every scan against the timber. In the first year of a plateau I would use my existing modelling tool, then put a new sum from my wages into our workshop fund each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I enjoy the tools, but the roof is interesting even when they only save me an hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why add money to the workshop fund?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our grown children no longer need help with rent, so I can put part of my current pay aside for a better bench. That is new saving, not money shifted from another account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the scanner ever settle a repair decision?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, it shows a shape. I sound the oak and check the joint before I tell the crew which timber can stay.

say: I would show the **mill joint** while explaining that roof scans still need inspection.
I would keep using my **existing AI model** to help with reports.
think: Healthy **repair contracts** and two wages support our savings.
A **scanner image** cannot decide whether an old timber is sound.
do: Lead the **church roof repair** and check every scan against the wood.
Add **new wage savings** to our workshop fund each month.
feel: **Calm**, because the tools help and the repair work remains absorbing.
S0.quote: I sound the oak and check the joint before I tell the crew which timber can stay.
fieldNote: Jamal already uses **AI modelling** daily, so continuing it is ordinary work rather than new learning.
He adds **fresh savings from pay** to a workshop fund because grown children need less support.

steps.text: Lead the church roof repair and check scans against timber
Add part of each wage to the workshop fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew we should test new machines on replaceable workshop stock before anyone touches a listed building. I would also show apprentices how I compare an AI cut list with a hand measurement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Faster tender writing might bring us more bids, but other firms could undercut us and trim our paid site hours. My side furniture orders could grow or fall, depending on whether buyers still value hand finishing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the firm for a paid place on the new robot-control course and apply if one opens. After completion, I would apply for any posted local heritage-tech lead role that pays at least my current rate; if no such post appears, I would keep taking our repair contracts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious and curious. My savings are substantial, but a long run of cheaper bids could reduce the pay we count on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes the workshop trial safe enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Use new timber away from the site, fence the arm, and test the stop before anyone feeds a joint through. A qualified supervisor must sign the setup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the course alone move you into the new role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I need an offered paid place first, and then an actual local vacancy at the right wage. A certificate does not create a job.

say: I would request a **fenced workshop trial** before robots approach historic timber.
I would teach apprentices to check an **AI cut list** by hand.
think: Cheaper bids might reduce **paid site hours**, even if tenders get quicker.
My **furniture orders** could move either way as buyers choose between methods.
do: Apply for a **paid robot-control course** only if a place is offered.
Apply for a **posted local lead job** after completion only if it matches my wage.
Keep taking **repair contracts** if no suitable vacancy appears.
feel: **Anxious** about possible cuts to paid site hours and furniture income, while remaining curious about new tools.
S1.quote: A certificate does not create a job.
fieldNote: His adaptive interest becomes a **conditional course application** and a separate job application after completion.
He insists on a **safe workshop setup**, an offered paid place and a posted comparable-wage vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the conservation officer that thinking AI in 2028 can draw a repair, but it cannot sound a beam. A capable robot around 2031 needs a documented trial away from the old roof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be sixty when the thinking system comes and sixty three when robots can handle the work. We could afford a gap, but a sudden drop in contracts would put my remaining good wages and my small furniture sales at risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would list our essential bills with Lucia and ask the firm about its next two tenders. If my paid site days fall for two months, I would apply to posted local carpentry jobs only where the wage and safety duties are clear; I would keep the furniture workshop small until orders justify more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a quick loss of two income streams. I like new tools, yet speed gives us little room to see which contracts survive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the new robot can cut an exact joint?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would still keep it off irreplaceable beams until a qualified person checks the material and the fixing. Accuracy on new wood does not prove safety in an old roof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire straight away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. We would price the gap first, and I would keep working while contracts and my health permit. A frightening card is not proof our savings cover an early exit.

say: I would tell the officer **2028 AI** can draw repairs before capable robots arrive around 2031.
I would require a **documented safety trial** away from old roof timbers.
think: A sudden **contract drop** could cut my last good wages.
Our **furniture sales** might weaken at the same time, though savings cover a gap.
do: List **essential bills** with Lucia and ask about the next two tenders.
Apply for **posted local carpentry work** after two shorter months only with clear wages and safety duties.

feel: **Anxious** about losing both site pay and furniture sales quickly.
S2.quote: Accuracy on new wood does not prove safety in an old roof.
fieldNote: Jamal is willing to adopt tools, yet his **historic roof safety** threshold remains strict.
He links a possible **job application** to two weak months, a posted vacancy and clear pay conditions.

steps.text: Apply after two shorter months to posted local carpentry jobs with clear wages and safety duties

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years lets us test the machines on timber that can be replaced. The restoration firm should give younger carpenters paid time to learn both the scanner and the hand joint.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be sixty three at the 2031 thinking date and sixty six when capable robots follow. I may have left full-time site work before then if Lucia and I can cover our bills, though I would like to keep making occasional furniture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask the firm for a funded place and paid hours on a new robotic joinery course. If I complete it and a posted local conservation-tech vacancy pays at least my current rate, I would apply; if already retired in the first year after 2031, I would work only on workshop orders I have actually received.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful but uneasy about younger workers. Younger carpenters need a paid place to practise rather than a video.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you put a robot onto the church roof after the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. It would start with new workshop timber behind guards and a qualified supervisor. Site use would need a separate approval and a demonstrated safe method.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course is not funded?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would continue my existing scanner work and hand repairs while the firm has contracts. I would not assume I can buy my way into an unposted vacancy.

say: I would argue for **paid practice time** in scanning and hand joinery.
I would keep robots on **replaceable workshop timber** until a separate site approval.
think: At **sixty three**, I may already have left full-time site work if our income allows.
Younger carpenters still need **funded practical access** to learn safe methods.
do: Request a **funded course place** and paid practice hours now.
Apply for a **posted conservation-tech role** after completion only at comparable pay.
Work on **actual workshop orders** after 2031 if retired from site work.
feel: **Uneasy** for younger workers, alongside hope that paid training can work.
S3.quote: Younger carpenters need a paid place to practise rather than a video.
fieldNote: The funded course, practice hours and later **vacancy application** are distinct conditional steps.
He separates **current site work** from possible workshop orders after 2031 if retired.

steps.text: Apply for robotic joinery course if funded place and paid hours open

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the apprentices that a decade is enough to learn timber diagnosis and the new controls side by side. Even in 2039, an old roof deserves a qualified inspection before a robot touches it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be sixty eight when thinking AI arrives in 2036 and seventy one when capable robots follow. I expect regular roof work to be over by then if our household income and health permit, while furniture commissions may still give me something to make.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now, in 2026, I would teach the apprentice to cut and check a scarf joint and continue the current roof contract. In the first year after 2036, if retired from site work, I would accept only commissions that pay for my time; if still employed, I would use new machines only after site approval and a safe method.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the runway, with some worry for starters. The first paid job is where a carpenter learns what drawings leave out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you promise the apprentice a job in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I can teach while our firm has a paid place, but I cannot promise a vacancy ten years from now. I can show what a sound joint feels like today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you enlarge the workshop now for 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after steady paid orders cover the cost and Lucia and I review our retirement income. I will not spend savings on an imagined robot market.

I would require **qualified inspection** before 2039 robots enter an old roof.
think: I expect to leave **regular roof work** before 2036 if income and health allow.
Future **furniture commissions** remain possible, with no guaranteed orders.
do: Teach the **apprentice** a scarf joint on the current 2026 contract.
Accept **paid commissions** after 2036 if retired; use approved equipment if still employed.
feel: **Calm** about time, with concern for apprentices entering the trade.
S4.quote: The first paid job is where a carpenter learns what drawings leave out.
fieldNote: His ten-year plan starts with **2026 paid work** and practical teaching on a real contract.
He distinguishes **conditional retirement** from work after 2036, and will expand only after paid orders justify it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Which picture worries you most, and what would help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because site tenders and table orders could both fall before I have time to change course. A funded paid training place, real safety trials and clear local vacancies would give me choices.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: What else should I have asked?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask how apprentices will get their first paid hours if machines take the carrying and rough cuts. A young carpenter needs a real joint to check, not just a perfect model.

headlineQuote: A young carpenter needs a real joint to check, not just a perfect model.
portrait: **Jamal**, 58, is a senior restoration carpenter with a vocational trade certificate and daily use of roof scanning and AI modelling.
His **higher pay**, paid house, substantial savings and Lucia’s clinic income support a flexible retirement plan.
He has **many nearby construction jobs** and a small furniture side business, but checks actual pay and orders before changing course.
His **adaptive approach** combines interest in controls training with strict site safety and funded paid practice conditions.
biggestWorry: A fast **2028 contract decline** could cut both Jamal’s site wages and his furniture orders.
whatWouldHelp: Funded **paid training**, demonstrated safety and posted local jobs at clear wages would help him adapt.
